verdict.rationale: GrowthBook's docs say metrics are created mainly through Fact Tables, where you write SQL against your own warehouse and define multiple metrics on top of those rows. It is warehouse-native across 11 data sources. Independent users confirm it queries existing warehouse or click-stream data rather than requiring events pushed into a walled-garden metric store. missing for 10: evidence of a first-party ingested-events path (the managed no-warehouse option is only hinted at on pricing), deeper documentation of metric definition types and options.

support.subject: As a product manager, I can define experiment metrics from my own data — warehouse tables or ingested events — instead of a black-box metric store

citations.quote: The primary way to create metrics in GrowthBook is with **Fact Tables** where you write SQL to pull a set of rows and then define multiple metrics on top of those rows.
Define Fact Tables and metrics so GrowthBook can compute experiment results from your warehouse.
Warehouse Native. Query 11 data sources including BigQuery, Snowflake, and Databricks.
GrowthBook (like Eppo) connects to your existing data warehouse and supports any metric you can express as a query.
They expose views over their own click-stream data, so they keep one high-quality data source instead of sending data to third-party tools
